analysis.investment_thesis: Cyient serves structurally attractive end-markets — aerospace, defense, utilities, semiconductors — and has grown revenue from 4,534 Cr to 7,360 Cr between FY22–FY25. However, thin 9% operating margins, a troubling decline in both EBITDA and net profit in FY25 vs FY24, and a dangerously low promoter holding of 23% make this a business I cannot own with high conviction.
key_strengths: Revenue grew from 4,534 Cr (FY22) to 7,360 Cr (FY25) — 17.5% CAGR — driven by aerospace, defense and utilities verticals that ride India's and global industrial spending cycles
Near debt-free (D/E 0.07) with cash of 1,067 Cr and consistent positive OCF across all 5 years; clean balance sheet limits downside
Forward P/E of 14.6x and EV/EBITDA of 13.6x offer reasonable valuation if margins recover, providing limited downside from current levels
key_risks: EBITDA fell from 1,376 Cr (FY24) to 1,224 Cr (FY25) and net profit dropped from 703 Cr to 648 Cr — a business losing operating leverage despite revenue growth is a serious yellow flag
Operating margin of only 9% for an engineering services company is thin and leaves almost no room for error; global IT services peers earn 18-25% margins
Finance costs have grown from 16 Cr (FY16) to 93 Cr (FY25) at a 21.6% CAGR — well above revenue growth, indicating increasing leverage in the business
red_flags: Promoter holding of only 23.28% is a major red flag for me — I need founders or families with significant skin in the game; at this level, there is little alignment between promoters and minority shareholders
Other income collapsed from 112–158 Cr range (FY16–FY20) to near zero by FY24 — stripping a key earnings cushion that may have masked underlying profitability weakness
Net profit in FY25 (648 Cr) declined from FY24 (703 Cr) despite higher revenues — negative operating leverage is unacceptable in a services business
analysis.detailed_analysis:
Cyient is an engineering services and Design-Led Manufacturing (DLM) company serving genuinely attractive global industries — aerospace, defense, rail, utilities. The recent revenue acceleration is real. But the quality of earnings concerns me deeply: operating margins at 9% are well below any peer I would consider investing in, and the FY25 PAT decline on higher revenues means the company is either facing pricing pressure, higher employee costs, or DLM segment drag. The 9-year net profit CAGR of 8.2% is disappointing given the tailwinds in its end markets.

The biggest dealbreaker for me as a long-term investor is the promoter holding of just 23.28%. In India, promoter conviction is everything — when promoters hold less than 25%, I start questioning whether they are building a legacy or managing an exit. The DII holding of 39.51% keeps the stock from falling too far, but this does not substitute for founder-led growth energy. I would need to see sustained margin recovery to 12-14%, promoter holding stability, and at least two quarters of PAT growth before revisiting.
